name: Differentiable particle filters (DPFs): Chen & Li survey (2023); conditional-normalizing-flow DPF (2021) and normalizing-flow DPF (2024/25); StateMixNN learned Gaussian-mixture proposals (2024/25); semi-supervised DPF (ICRA 2021, revisited 2024); Mixture Density Particle Filter (NeurIPS 2023); PyDPF library (2025)
authors_org: Xiongjie Chen & Yunpeng Li (Univ. of Surrey / King's College London) for the survey, CNF-DPF and NF-DPF; Hao Wen, Xiongjie Chen, Georgios Papagiannis, Conghui Hu, Yunpeng Li (semi-supervised DPF); Benjamin Cox, Santiago Segarra, Victor Elvira (StateMixNN, Edinburgh / Rice); Ali Younis & Erik Sudderth (UC Irvine, MDPF); John-Joseph Brady, Benjamin Cox, Victor Elvira, Yunpeng Li (PyDPF). Foundations: Jonschkowski et al. (RSS 2018), Karkus et al. PF-net (CoRL 2018), Corenflos et al. OT resampling (ICML 2021).
year: 2021-2025 (survey 2023; CNF-DPF 2021; semi-supervised DPF 2020/2021, revisited 2024; MDPF 2023; NF-DPF arXiv 2024, TSP 2025; StateMixNN arXiv 2024, Signal Processing 2025; PyDPF 2025)

Semi-supervised DPF: ICRA 2021, arXiv:2011.05748 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.05748); revisited objectives arXiv:2405.01251. MDPF: NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2404.08789 (https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/85b2ff7574ef265f3a4800db9112ce14-Abstract-Conference.html). PyDPF: arXiv:2510.25693 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25693).
code_availability: Yes for several: PyDPF (PyTorch, unified API over many DPF variants) https://github.com/John-JoB/pydpf; NF-DPF https://github.com/xiongjiechen/Normalizing-Flows-DPFs. MDPF and StateMixNN code availability [uncertain] (not linked from the arXiv abstract pages). Our own non-differentiable PF: rogii_champion/src/particle_filter.py; exact grid HMM: kaggle2ndplace/anchor_hmm.py; the failed post-hoc forward-backward decode: kaggle_1st_place/solution/posterior_fb_decode.py.
evidence_level: Peer-reviewed (ICRA, NeurIPS, IEEE TSP, Signal Processing, FoDS) plus arXiv preprints; no application to well logs, geosteering or ROGII found. Relevance judgements below are our analysis, not reported results.
extreme_summary: DPFs make the particle filter's transition, proposal and measurement models neural networks and train them end-to-end through the filter (differentiable or gradient-corrected resampling), so the emission model is learned for use inside sequential inference rather than in isolation. For us the valuable idea is not the particles (a 1D TVT state is solved exactly on a grid) but training / tempering the U-Net posterior so that it composes correctly with a sequential dip-aware tracker.
task_definition: Sequential Bayesian state estimation (filtering / smoothing) in state-space models whose dynamics and observation likelihood are unknown or high-dimensional (images), learning those models from data; benchmark tasks are robot localisation (maze / house environments), visual object tracking and synthetic nonlinear SSMs.
inputs: Observation sequences (images, sensor readings, low-dimensional synthetic observations) and optionally actions; labelled state trajectories for supervised variants, few or no labels for semi-supervised / likelihood-trained variants (SDPF, StateMixNN). In a ROGII transfer the observation at each MD column would be the lateral GR window plus the typewell, or directly the U-Net per-column posterior.
target_parameterisation: Explicit latent state x_t (pose, object position, generic hidden state). A ROGII instance would use (TVT level, structural slope r = dS/dMD with S = TVT + Z, optional GR bias), the same state as our PF.
output_representation: Weighted particle set, i.e. an empirical (multimodal) posterior per step; MDPF turns it into a continuous kernel-mixture density; NF-DPF gives valid normalised densities; StateMixNN uses Gaussian-mixture proposal and transition densities. Point estimates are usually the weighted particle mean.
architecture: Classical PF loop with neural components: (1) dynamic model p_theta(x_t | x_{t-1}) as an MLP-parameterised Gaussian / mixture or a conditional normalizing flow; (2) proposal q_phi(x_t | x_{t-1}, y_t) that looks at the latest observation (CNF-DPF, NF-DPF, StateMixNN Gaussian mixtures) instead of the bootstrap proposal; (3) measurement model l_psi(y_t | x_t) as a learned feature-similarity network or a conditional flow density; (4) differentiable resampling: soft resampling (Karkus 2018), entropy-regularised optimal-transport resampling (Corenflos 2021), or none/stop-gradient; MDPF instead represents the posterior as a kernel mixture and uses an importance-sampling gradient estimator so resampling gradients are unbiased and low variance. PyDPF implements these variants behind one PyTorch API.
core_mechanism: End-to-end learning through the filter: the loss is computed on the filter's output (e.g. RMSE of the weighted mean against ground truth, or the marginal log-likelihood / ELBO of observations), so the measurement model is trained to be a good likelihood for sequential fusion, including its sharpness (temperature) relative to the dynamics; algorithmic structure (predict-update-resample) acts as a prior that reduces data needs. MDPF adds that multimodal posteriors can be tracked stably over long horizons when gradients through resampling are unbiased, whereas truncated-gradient DPFs are unstable and lose modes.
training_objective: Supervised: RMSE / NLL of filtered state vs ground-truth trajectories (Jonschkowski 2018, MDPF NLL of the mixture density). Unsupervised / semi-supervised: marginal log-likelihood of observations estimated by the filter (StateMixNN), pseudo-likelihood on unlabelled sequences plus supervised loss on labelled ones (SDPF), ELBO-style objectives; revisited-objectives paper (2405.01251) compares two semi-supervised losses and finds neither uniformly better [uncertain on exact conclusion].
decoding: Weighted particle mean (most common) or mixture-density statistics; smoothing variants use backward passes. For RMSE the weighted mean of the (smoothed) posterior is the right summary.
metric_consistent_decode: RMSE-consistent when the weighted mean is used and trained with RMSE; mode-seeking only if a best-particle / MAP summary is taken. The real risk for us is not the decode but an over-confident fused posterior (see gap field), which makes the mean behave like an arg-max.
evidence_scope: Sequence-level: causal filtering over the whole trajectory, optional smoothing (whole sequence). No multi-sequence (multi-well) evidence sharing.
prefix_conditioning: Not addressed in the literature beyond initial-state priors; in ROGII the known heel prefix would set a tight initial distribution at the last known row and an initial slope estimate (as our PF already does via _initial_rate).
propose_vs_select: Produces a full posterior per step, so it can serve as a candidate path, an input channel, or a posterior re-weighting of the U-Net output; it slots in as an ensemble member or as a decode stage.
physical_constraints: Only whatever the dynamic model encodes; in our transfer: smooth structural slope random walk (dip), rare fault jumps, S = TVT + Z identity, GR bias drift. Learned dynamics could learn well-type-specific dip statistics from training wells.
dataset: Robotics / vision benchmarks: DeepMind Lab maze localisation, House3D, KITTI-style visual odometry, disk / object tracking, synthetic linear-Gaussian and stochastic-volatility SSMs. No geoscience data.
synthetic_to_real: Mostly synthetic or simulated; SDPF evaluates on a real robot dataset. For us the relevant point is that DPF emissions are trained on the same distribution they are applied to, whereas our U-Net is trained on 85% synthetic wells, so any learned temperature / emission scaling should be fitted on real training wells only.
metric_and_performance: Survey: qualitative taxonomy, no new numbers. MDPF: reported large accuracy and stability gains over truncated-gradient DPFs and RNNs on long-range tracking and localisation (exact numbers not extracted) [uncertain]. StateMixNN: better hidden-state recovery than prior NN-SSM baselines, strongest in highly nonlinear models. NF-DPF / CNF-DPF: lower tracking error than bootstrap DPFs on synthetic and visual tracking tasks. Our related baselines on 155 holdout wells: hand-tuned PF 15.84 ft standalone (after slope-walk x9 and drift calibration), AnchorCNN + PF channels 5.84 ft (C_s1_pfchan), post-hoc forward-backward over ConvNeXt posteriors 11.32 -> 12.14 ft on 16 focus wells (worse).
comparability: Not comparable: different domains and metrics (pose RMSE, NLL). Only our own PF / HMM / fb-decode numbers are on the 155-well holdout.
validation_protocol: Standard train / test splits of simulated trajectories; multiple training seeds in MDPF (stability across runs is a headline result). No spatial grouping issues. For us any learned emission scaling must be fitted on training wells and scored on the holdout with seq_NN_robust_compare.py paired bootstrap.
inference_budget: Cheap for a 1D/2D state: a grid HMM over 400 levels x ~50 slopes x 345 columns is ~7M multiply-adds per well (anchor_hmm.py runs 0.11 s/well at 129 x 53); a 512-particle PF is tens of ms per well. Training a DPF end-to-end adds a sequential loop over 345 columns per well to the backward pass, which is slow in Python but fine if written as batched log-sum-exp on the grid.
repeated_layers: Particles or mixture components can keep several band hypotheses alive; MDPF specifically targets stable tracking of multiple posterior modes. But a filter can only resolve band confusion if the sequence contains disambiguating evidence the per-column posterior has not already used; the U-Net's receptive field already spans the whole 345-column image, so most of that evidence is already inside each column posterior. Our PF notes: mode collapse was ruled out (512 vs 4096 particles moved results 0.02 ft) and 'the posterior genuinely prefers the wrong layer', i.e. an evidence limit.
drift: An explicit slope state is the natural fix for one-straight-line-per-well drift: a tracker with dip momentum extrapolates the heel dip and corrects it as evidence accumulates. Our PF showed the slope prior is the dominant knob (slope walk x9: 28.98 -> 16.82 ft) and that a residual linear drift remained (calibrated -0.0026 ft/ft). The failed posterior_fb_decode.py has NO slope state (zero-mean level kernel), so a dip-aware version is untested.
uncertainty_and_calibration: Filtered posterior spread is the uncertainty output; DPF training with NLL (MDPF) calibrates the mixture. No reliability / ECE analysis in the surveyed papers. Key for us: fusing N column posteriors assumes conditionally independent emissions; ours are highly correlated (shared receptive field), so the raw product is badly over-confident unless tempered.
where_to_use: (1) Decode stage after the ConvNeXt / FastViT: treat per-column posteriors p_t(level) as scaled likelihoods (p_t / prior)^tau inside an exact grid HMM over (level, slope), take the expectation of the smoothed marginal. (2) Training-time: a differentiable forward-backward layer on the posterior grid with an RMSE loss on the smoothed mean (DPF-style end-to-end training), learning tau and the transition parameters. (3) As a PF-channel generator that uses the network's posterior (instead of raw GR likelihood) as the measurement model, feeding back into a second-stage network.
error_mode_targeted: Drift (~25%) via the slope state; band confusion (~51%) only through calibration of how evidence is fused (tempering), not through new evidence.
gap_vs_our_implementation: What we have: a bootstrap PF with hand-set Student-t GR likelihood (rogii_champion/src/particle_filter.py; 3 profiles x 512 particles; state L, r, b; genealogy smoothing), an exact grid HMM on GR (anchor_hmm.py, ~23 ft, not competitive), PF channels to AnchorCNN (5.84 ft), and a post-hoc forward-backward decode over ConvNeXt posteriors that failed (posterior_fb_decode.py). What the DPF literature offers that we do not do: (a) LEARNED emission scaling. posterior_fb_decode.py multiplies the raw per-column softmax outputs directly (exponent 1, no division by the training prior). Because every column posterior already integrates evidence from the whole lateral, multiplying ~345 of them counts the same evidence hundreds of times, making the fused posterior extremely peaked; the smoothed mean then behaves like an arg-max and inherits arg-max's wrong-band losses, exactly the failure its docstring reports ('wins where it locks onto the right band, loses where it locks onto a wrong one'). DPF training (or simply fitting a temperature tau on training wells) is the principled correction; hybrid NN-HMM practice divides posteriors by the class prior to get scaled likelihoods. This knob has not been tried. (b) A slope / dip state in the decode: our fb decode uses a zero-mean level random walk, so it cannot represent the per-well straight-line drift that is ~25% of error and worth 1.9 ft (per-well linear-trend oracle 4.94 -> 3.07 ft on ConvNeXt). (c) End-to-end training through the sequential layer (the network never sees the smoother during training, so it is not trained to produce posteriors that compose). (d) Mode-preserving posterior representations (MDPF mixtures) - low priority because our 1D state is exact on a grid, so particles and differentiable resampling solve a problem we do not have. Confirmation of what we already do: bootstrap PF with fault jumps, slope state, GR bias, backward smoothing, multi-profile blending - all present.
proposed_experiment: E1 (no training, 1-2 h, decides whether E2 is worth it): new script kaggle_1st_place/solution/posterior_hmm_decode.py extending posterior_fb_decode.py: state = (level on the 400-level posterior grid, slope r on ~41 bins spanning [-0.05, 0.05] ft/ft); transition: level_t = level_{t-1} + r*dMD - dZ + N(0, s_L), r random walk N(0, s_r) (reuse the S = TVT + Z convention of particle_filter.py); emission = (p_t(level) / pi(level))^tau with pi the training-set marginal of levels (or uniform); initial state from the heel prefix and _initial_rate. Fit tau in {0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0}, s_r, s_L on TRAINING-well posteriors (dump them with seq_NN_posterior_dump.py --save-all on a training subset), then score once on the 155 holdout wells from results/baseline_check_posterior_all (expectation of smoothed marginal vs raw expectation). Also report the blend 'mean of raw expectation and HMM expectation' and the per-well linear-trend residual to see whether drift shrinks. Control: raw expectation decode of the same dump (5.47 ft at 60 epochs; repeat on the 4.84 ft FastViT dump). Accept only if paired bootstrap gain > 0.39 ft or consistent gain on both dumps. E2 (only if E1 shows tau << 1 helps): make the grid HMM a differentiable layer (log-space forward-backward with torch.logsumexp over level and slope; banded transition as a 1D convolution) placed after the U-Net softmax, learnable tau, s_r, s_L; fine-tune the FastViT student 20-30 epochs from its checkpoint with loss = RMSE of smoothed mean + existing per-column loss (keep the per-column KD term so distillation is untouched); control = same fine-tune schedule without the layer. E3 (cheap diagnostic): on holdout wells tagged wrong_mode by the error-anatomy script, check whether the tempered HMM's smoothed marginal puts more mass on the true band than the raw column posterior; if not, stop - the evidence is not there.
implementation_effort: Low for E1 (numpy, ~150 lines, reuse posterior_fb_decode.py I/O); medium for E2 (differentiable banded 2D forward-backward in torch, memory care over 345 columns x 400 levels x 41 slopes, plus a fine-tune run); low for E3.
gpu_cost: E1: CPU only, seconds per well (~7M ops per well for 400 x 41 x 345), minutes for all 155 wells plus a training-well sweep. E2: forward-backward tensor per well ~345 x 400 x 41 floats = 5.7M (23 MB fp32, x2-3 for autograd) - fits in 8 GB at batch 4-8; a 20-30 epoch fine-tune of FastViT-SA12 is roughly 15-25% of a full 150-epoch run [uncertain].
distillation_compatibility: E1 is a post-hoc decode, fully compatible (applies to teacher or student posteriors). E2 adds a layer after the softmax; KD on per-column posteriors can stay on the pre-HMM output while the HMM loss acts on the smoothed mean, so the FastViT + KD recipe is preserved.
error_correlation_with_ours: Low diversity: the decode reuses our own posterior, so it corrects our errors rather than adding an independent member; it cannot fix wells where the posterior has no mass on the true band. A GR-likelihood PF (our existing one) is the decorrelated member (residual corr 0.27-0.34) but too weak (15.8 ft) to earn weight.
risk: (1) Metric fact from context: for pooled RMSE the expectation of a calibrated posterior is already Bayes-optimal, so a smoother only helps if the per-column posterior is miscalibrated relative to the path-level posterior or if the slope prior adds information (dip continuity) the network ignores; the prior fb decode failed, and tempering may just converge back to the raw mean as tau -> 0 (a null result is likely). (2) Evidence double counting cannot be removed exactly by a single scalar tau; the right exponent varies with well length and posterior sharpness. (3) Mode-seeking lock-in reappears if tau is too large. (4) E2 end-to-end training is the trained version of B05's neural CRF and overlaps with it; 60-epoch structured experiments (AcfNet target, axial attention, RAFT) all failed here, so expect a small effect within the +-0.39 ft noise floor. (5) DPF papers solve high-dimensional-state / unknown-likelihood problems; our state is 1-2D and our likelihood is already a strong learned network, so most DPF machinery (differentiable resampling, flows) is irrelevant.
notes: Mapping to our stack: the U-Net per-column softmax IS a learned measurement model in DPF terms (PF-net / Jonschkowski style), and 400 discrete levels make the exact grid filter preferable to particles (no resampling variance, trivially differentiable). The distinctive DPF lesson worth importing is to train or calibrate the emission for use inside the sequential model (MDPF: NLL-trained mixtures stay multimodal and stable). Semi-supervised DPF (pseudo-likelihood on unlabelled sequences) suggests a transductive option: use the unlabelled parts of holdout / test laterals to fit tau and slope noise by marginal likelihood without labels - fold-safe because no TVT is used, but only worth trying after E1. Related items: A05 (Bayesian / PF geosteering), B05 (differentiable DP / neural CRF), B09 (calibration), B10 (test-time adaptation on the prefix).
